post_resolution_check.notes: Reversal of speaking subject at the response formula is consistently applied here as elsewhere in ch.1; content shift from charge to oath-vow supports the seam. Fine.

primary_reviews.rationale: Dispatch clause and gate-shutting clause are both verbatim. The narrative precis around them is not accurate: 2:2 is impersonal, וַיֵּ֣אָמַ֔ר לְמֶ֥לֶךְ יְרִיח֖וֹ, a report reaching the king rather than an inquiry issuing from him, and 2:3 is a demand (ה֠וֹצִיאִי), while concealment on the roof in v.6 comes after the ruse of vv.4-5, not before it as the summary's ordering implies. Neither slip touches an edge, and the cause-and-effect argument for stopping at v.7 rather than v.6 holds: the pursuers leaving and the gate closing are the ruse paying off. Far edge is independently marked by the disjunctive clause opening v.8.

primary_reviews.rationale: The טֶ֣רֶם clause is quoted correctly and does the work claimed for it - fronted independent pronoun plus a pre-durative negation, which is how this narrator resets to a scene he stepped away from. The far edge is the softer one, since v.15 continues in mainline wayyiqtol rather than breaking, and the medium_low price already registers that asymmetry. I found no stronger seam inside vv.8-14: v.9's וַתֹּ֨אמֶר֙ and v.12's וְעַתָּ֗ה are turns within one speech, and v.14's answering formula belongs to the same exchange.

That supports isolating vv.8-14 as its own movement despite unbroken location and participants. The unit closes cleanly on the mutual life-pledge in v.14, immediately before v.15 shifts into a new narrated register.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: Reading טֶ֣רֶם יִשְׁכָּב֑וּן as a cutaway-and-return marker rather than a bare time-stamp is defensible - the fronted independent pronoun plus pre-durative negation does the narrative work both primaries claim for it - and medium_low honestly reflects that the far edge (the shift to v.15's narrated action) is considerably softer than the near one.

post_resolution_check.notes: Resumptive טרם marker correctly read as pulling back to the roof after the gate cutaway; medium_low is earned since the far edge (v.15's narrated act) is the real closural signal, not a formula.

primary_reviews.rationale: Both anchors match, though the rationale's spelling of the window drops the meteg that MT and the row's own evidence ref both carry (הַֽחַלּ֑וֹן against הַחַלּ֑וֹן). The letting-down is announced first, then the escape-route and cord-sign instructions that logically accompany or precede it are given in direct speech through v.20, before v.21 closes the physical action (tying the cord) that v.15 already named. That headline-then-elaborate pattern is a recognized way Hebrew narrative presents overlapping action, and it gives the vv.15-21 split firmer footing than 'breaks the dialogue' alone, since v.15 is doing double duty as both an action notice and the opening frame for what follows.

primary_reviews.rationale: The return clause and the closing report are exact. The inclusio claim understates itself: 2:9 and 2:24 share not a theme but a four-word string, נָמֹ֛גוּ כָּל יֹשְׁבֵ֥י הָאָ֖רֶץ, differing only in the pronoun that flips the perspective from Rahab's מִפְּנֵיכֶֽם to the spies' מִפָּנֵֽינוּ. That is as hard an inclusio as this chapter offers and it deserves to be quoted rather than paraphrased. Near edge is a genuine double relocation, far edge is the samekh plus 3:1's new-day formula.

That is a mechanically verifiable refrain closing the chapter, not a loose thematic echo, and it is the strongest single piece of evidence in this cluster for a clean far edge.

primary_reviews.rationale: Rise-early formula and three-day time-stamp are both verbatim. The row's reading of v.2 as connective tissue rather than an independent unit is defensible and I can add a reason it does not give: v.1 itself ends on a lodging notice, וַיָּלִ֥נוּ שָׁ֖ם טֶ֥רֶם יַעֲבֹֽרוּ, so vv.1-2 already form a bracketed interval - arrival, overnight, three days elapsed - before any speech begins. Far edge is 3:3's command formula. That same lodging-clause pattern becomes decisive against the draft at 6:11, where it is not acknowledged.

The boundary_rationale describes v.2 as 'connective tissue bridging the march notice to the command' but then assigns it to the march notice (v.1) rather than to the command it bridges toward - that placement runs against the sentence's own logic. Grammatically v.2 has two parts: the וַיְהִי מִקְצֵה שְׁלֹשֶׁת יָמִים time marker, and then וַיַּעַבְרוּ הַשֹּׁטְרִים בְּקֶרֶב הַמַּחֲנֶה ('the officers passed through the camp'). It is that second clause, naming the officers as subject, that carries directly into v.3's וַיְצַוּוּ אֶת הָעָם ('and they commanded the people') - same subject, one continuous action of moving through camp in order to issue a command. Participant-and-action continuity favors grouping 3:2b with 3:3-4 over grouping it with 3:1's arrival-and-lodging notice. I also note the identical וַיְהִי + temporal-phrase construction is elsewhere in this draft treated as a scene-opening formula (1:1, 3:14, 4:1, 5:13), which cuts against reading it here as backward-looking connective tissue.

challenges.claim: The boundary_rationale's own description of 3:2 as 'connective tissue bridging the march notice to the command' actually supports attaching v.2 to the following officers'-command unit (3:3-4), not to the preceding arrival notice (3:1); the officers introduced as subject in 3:2b are the same subject who issue the command in 3:3, an unbroken participant-and-action chain the current span cuts across.
challenges.suggested_action: Reconsider the near edge of 3:1-3:2: either re-draw the span as 3:1 alone, with 3:2-4 forming the officers' mobilization-and-command unit, or add explicit justification for why v.2's forward-pointing bridge function does not outweigh participant continuity into v.3.

primary_reviews.rationale: Checked against both neighbours, the retreat to a one-verse span is the right call and the row pays for it honestly. 3:1 is a closed arrival report: rise, journey from Shittim, arrival at the Jordan, overnight lodging before crossing. What decides the far edge is not that bracket but what happens on the other side of it: מִקְצֵ֖ה שְׁלֹ֣שֶׁת יָמִ֑ים brings the officers on stage, and 3:3's command verb takes them over with no subject named again, so v.2 cannot be detached from v.3 without breaking a single chain. The row states the competing continuity in its own ALT rather than burying it, and medium_low is the correct price for a boundary chosen between two live readings. Nothing here leans on a parashah site or on WEB formatting.

As a literary unit this is a clean arrival-and-encampment beat: rise early, march from Shittim, reach the Jordan, camp overnight before crossing. The bracketing clause וַיָּלִ֥נוּ שָׁ֖ם טֶ֥רֶם יַעֲבֹֽרוּ genuinely closes the beat rather than merely trailing off, and I independently checked the wayyiqtol chain into v.3: v.2's הַשֹּׁטְרִים are indeed the grammatical subject that carries straight into v.3's command with no reintroduced subject, so reading v.2 forward with the officers rather than back with the encampment notice is the better call. The row is honest that v.1's own closural bracket is a live competing signal, which is the right way to hold a medium_low call rather than overselling it.
evidence_refs: oshb:Josh.3.2-3 (wayyiqtol chain, verified no subject reset)

peer_crosscheck.assessment: LF's challenge is right that the row talks past itself: it names v.2b as the bridge toward the officers' command and then places v.2 with v.1 anyway. The wayyiqtol chain is unbroken from 3:2b's וַיַּעַבְרוּ הַשֹּׁטְרִים into 3:3's וַיְצַוּוּ - same subject, no formula break - which is a stronger continuity signal than the frozen row credits. That said, OL's counter-observation deserves equal weight and is not addressed by the challenge: v.1 closes with its own bracketing clause, וַיָּלִנוּ שָׁם טֶרֶם יַעֲבֹרוּ, so an arrival-overnight-three-days interval genuinely exists on the other side of the seam too. primary_reviews.rationale: There is a real inconsistency in how the register-closure criterion gets applied here versus elsewhere in the surrounding decisions. V.9 closes with עַ֖ד הַיּ֥וֹם הַזֶּֽה ('there to this day'), and this exact closure formula is treated as decisive for marking a self-contained unit at 5:9 (the naming etiology, M8-Josh-024) and again at 6:22-25, where it is explicitly called 'Rahab's own inclusio-closing to this day formula' (M8-Josh-033). Here the identical construction closing v.9 is not given that weight; v.8 and v.9 are merged as one 'compressed fulfillment-register notice' because v.9 'lacks any independent speech-formula.' But the register-closure rule as stated privileges a discrete per-entry closure formula as decisive for content-differentiated entries, and v.9 has exactly that: an in-river stone-erection never actually commanded in vv.1-7, closed by its own to-this-day notice, genuinely differentiated in content from v.8's plain compliance report.

Worth noting for the record that this row's characterisation of 4:9 as a fronted-object qatal is the correct one, and it contradicts how M8-Josh-028 cites the same verse.

What makes this row work is its restraint: rather than harmonizing the second set of stones into the first (vv.1-8), it treats v.9 as its own etiological notice and openly names it an unexplained doublet with the preceding decision. That is honest handling of a genuine textual crux rather than a manufactured smoothing-over, and the 'to this day' closure - the same class credited at 5:9 and 6:25 - is a real, checkable closural device rather than an assumed one. medium_low is the right band for a boundary that is well-evidenced but whose relationship to its neighbor remains genuinely unresolved.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: This row's grammar claim and its closure claim both check out directly against the text: 4:9 opens on a fronted-object qatal, וּשְׁתֵּ֧ים עֶשְׂרֵ֣ה אֲבָנִ֗ים הֵקִ֣ים, with הֵקִים as a genuine finite verb (not a participle or verbless clause), and closes on עַ֖ד הַיּ֥וֹם הַזֶּֽה, the same closural device credited at 5:9 and 6:25 (both confirmed). OL's aside that this row's own accurate description of 4:9 as a fronted-object qatal 'contradicts how M8-Josh-028 cites the same verse' is worth flagging as independently confirmed rather than passed over: in a separate crosscheck of M8-Josh-028 I found that row had indeed cited Josh.4.9 as a verbless parallel to 6:1 before that claim was withdrawn in the r2 revision precisely because 4:9's הֵקִ֣ים is finite - this row and that correction now agree with each other, which is the right outcome. medium_low, resting on solid form but an unresolved relationship to the first stone-set, is well calibrated.

primary_reviews.rationale: I agree with the draft's central claim for the review brief's focus test: the 4:21-24 speech is a genuinely distinct occasion from 4:4-7, not a duplicate needing to be merged or excised. The addressee is now the nation generally rather than the twelve; the location is Gilgal rather than the riverbed; the framing has shifted to children asking 'their fathers' (v.21) rather than an unspecified 'you' (v.6); and the content is expanded into an explicit Red-Sea comparison and a purpose clause about all the earth's peoples knowing Yahweh's hand - a deliberately fuller, more theologically loaded answer to the same catechetical question, reading as intentional doubling rather than accident. Where I push back is on keeping vv.19-24 as a single 'movement': a fresh אמר-formula opens v.21 exactly like the formulas this draft treats as decisive splits earlier in ch.3 (3:5 split from 3:3-4, 3:6 split from 3:5), and the rationale here does not explain why that same signal is overridden by an 'arrival and explanation' framing rather than applied. The action-then-explanation reading is defensible but needs to be argued, not asserted, given how much weight formula-changes carry elsewhere in this cluster.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: LF is right that a fresh אמר-formula opens 4:21, but calling it 'the same category of signal' as 3:5 and 3:6 overstates the parallel: those verses (and 3:10, see M8-Josh-014) restate יְהוֹשֻׁעַ as an explicit subject, while 4:21's וַיֹּאמֶר אֶל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לֵאמֹר has no named subject at all and simply continues the referent already active from v.20. primary_reviews.rationale: The span is right and the singleton is genuinely free-standing - I take that focus question as answered in the draft's favour. What I dispute is medium_low. The row's echo claim, which I expected to be impressionistic, turns out to be verifiable and considerably tighter than stated: 5:1 does not merely recall the melting-heart theme, it reproduces two consecutive clauses of Rahab's speech, וַיִּמַּ֣ס לְבָבֵ֔נוּ becoming וַיִּמַּ֣ס לְבָבָ֗ם and וְלֹא קָ֨מָה ע֥וֹד ר֛וּחַ becoming וְלֹא הָ֨יָה בָ֥ם עוֹד֙ ר֔וּחַ. On top of that the near edge is a book-level type-scene opening that the draft itself identifies as recurrent at 9:1, and the far edge has both a samekh and 5:2's temporal-plus-messenger formula. Two independently evidenced edges plus a two-clause verbal echo is a medium case, and pricing it with the same hedged label used for genuinely thin rows flattens a distinction the reviewer downstream needs.

primary_reviews.rationale: On the specific question of whether 5:9 belongs with the Passover sequel: it should stand alone. The verse is a complete etiological unit in its own right - a divine word naming the place and explaining why, closed on its own 'to this day' formula, and its content (rolling away the reproach of Egypt, closing out a wilderness-generation theme) has nothing to do with v.10's topic, which is a calendar notice about keeping Passover with a fresh subject (בְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל rather than Yahweh) and no connecting particle at all. Folding it forward into 5:10-12 would blur two genuinely different genres - naming etiology versus ritual-calendar report - under one roof for no textual gain. Both edges are independently formula-evidenced even within a single verse, which is unusual and worth crediting at medium.

primary_reviews.rationale: The day-set works and the seventh-day seam at 6:15 holds cleanly. 6:12 reopens with the rise-early construction the campaign credits at 3:1 and 7:16 - I checked both and the verb-plus-subject-plus-ba-boqer shape is identical in all three. The far edge is doubly held: v.14 ends כֹּ֥ה עָשׂ֖וּ שֵׁ֥שֶׁת יָמִֽים, a summary sealing six days, and v.15 opens וַיְהִ֣י בַּיּ֣וֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִ֗י with a sevenfold circuit replacing the single one. Those two are independent of each other, which is more than the row claims for itself. Medium is if anything conservative, and I would not object to it staying there given the compressed-register judgement it also carries.

On the specific question of the far edge: it is right. I checked 6:15 directly and it opens with וַיְהִ֣י בַּיּ֣וֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִ֗י - 'and it happened on the seventh day' - a fresh temporal marker that unambiguously begins new, distinct content (the sevenfold circuit, trumpets, the shout) rather than continuing the compressed six-day summary. Compressing days two through six into one register while keeping the rise-early formula as the day-marker matches the pattern already established at v.12 and reused at 7:16, so this is a consistent application of a real recurring device rather than a one-off convenience split.

But one specific sentence in the rationale does not survive a direct check and neither reviewer caught it: it describes v.14's closure as 'its own return formula matching v.11's, וַיָּשֻׁ֖בוּ הַֽמַּחֲנֶ֑ה.' Josh.6.11 does not contain that phrase - it reads וַיָּבֹ֨אוּ֙ הַֽמַּחֲנֶ֔ה וַיָּלִ֖ינוּ בַּֽמַּחֲנֶֽה, a different verb root (בוא, 'came') from v.14's וַיָּשֻׁ֖בוּ (שוב, 'returned'). A full-book search confirms וַיָּשֻׁ֖בוּ הַֽמַּחֲנֶ֑ה occurs exactly once in Joshua, at 6:14 itself. This freeze's own row for v.11, M8-Josh-030, independently confirms the discrepancy: its rationale quotes v.11's actual closure as וַיָּבֹ֨אוּ֙ הַֽמַּחֲנֶ֔ה וַיָּלִ֖ינוּ בַּֽמַּחֲנֶֽה, not the phrase attributed to it here. This does not touch the boundary itself - the rise-early near edge and the six-day-summary-plus-seventh-day far edge are independently sound and unaffected - but the specific phrase-match claim is false as written and should be corrected (v.14 has its own distinct return-to-camp closure; it does not repeat v.11's wording).

That is a real construction, not a resemblance, and the row is careful to grade it as softer than a fresh wayyiqtol rather than trading up. The old claim of a wayyiqtol va-yomer at 6:22 is withdrawn explicitly. Closure at v.25 with the 'to this day' clause is present; the pe is called corroboration. Medium is well placed for a boundary held by a backgrounding construction plus a topic reopening.

The fronted-PP-plus-qatal opening (וְלִשְׁנַיִם הָאֲנָשִׁים... אָמַר יְהוֹשֻׁעַ) genuinely parallels 1:12's construction - I checked both and the shape matches down to the word order. The row is candid that this is a softer, topicalizing signal rather than a fresh wayyiqtol, and that honesty about signal strength is appropriate given the construction really is comparatively weaker than the mainline-formula splits used elsewhere. As a literary beat, reopening the Rahab plot here to discharge chapter 2's oath, then closing on the pe-corroborated 'to this day' notice, is a satisfying narrative payoff and a coherent unit regardless of the softer opening signal.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: Three challenges on this row, and adjudicating them requires separating admissible from inadmissible evidence before weighing anything. LF's challenge leans on a WEB paragraph break before 8:30 that I confirmed is real in the USFM source (a \p falls immediately before v.30), but under the mesh's own symmetry rule WEB paragraphing is metadata, not a driver, so that half of LF's case does not count toward re-pricing. What survives the strip is LF's other point, made independently and more precisely by OL: the frozen rationale calls the אָז-adverb 'loosely-connective' here while treating the identical construction as decisive enough to open a unit at 10:12 (058) two clusters later, an inconsistency in how one signal is weighted rather than a fact about the text. OL's grammar is the sharper version of this and I re-verified it directly against oshb: 8:30, 10:12, and 22:1 all pair אָז with a yiqtol (יִבְנֶה, יְדַבֵּר, יִקְרָא), while 10:33's אָז pairs with a qatal (עָלָה) and is left unit-internal by the draft's own hand. That is a real, discriminating distinction, not an assertion, and it means the near edge does not have 'no independently driving signal at all' as the rationale claims -- it has a comparative syntactic signal plus a total change of place to Mount Ebal. OL's participant claim also checks out: כָל יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ appears at 8:24 and וְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵ֡ל at 8:33, so the assertion that only Joshua carries over from the Ai narrative is false and should be struck. And the bookkeeping defect is exactly as OL describes it -- the frozen confidence is low, the rationale says it was re-priced to low, and the strongest_rejected_alternative still asserts a cap at medium_low, three inconsistent statements in one row. My own adjudication: the far edge is genuinely strong (pe, content shift, and 9:1's fresh type-scene formula all converge), and once the near edge is credited with the אָז-plus-yiqtol pattern rather than nothing, low is too severe. I do not think the near-edge signal is a full independent formula on the order of a new speech-marker, since crediting it requires comparing three other passages rather than reading this one in isolation, so I would not go all the way to medium either. Medium_low is the price this evidence actually supports, matching how the same cluster prices comparable one-strong-edge spans (052).

primary_reviews.rationale: This is a coherent deceptive-embassy type-scene (disguise, approach, presentation, interrogation, self-defense) at one location with one continuous cast, and the web:Josh.9.5 quotation ('old and patched sandals on their feet') matches the source exactly. WEB's paragraphing inside this span is granular - it opens a fresh paragraph at nearly every change of speaker within the vv.7-13 dialogue (Israel's challenge, the Gibeonites' 'we are your servants,' Joshua's question, their extended answer) - but that is ordinary quoted-dialogue formatting, not evidence of competing scene boundaries, since the location, participants, and topic never change across any of those breaks. This unit is a good candidate for the 'type-scene grammar' angle the review brief highlights: it inverts the Rahab/spy-reconnaissance pattern earlier in the book (outsiders investigate Israel there; here Israel is investigated by outsiders posing as distant petitioners), which the decision does not need to state but which supports reading vv.3-13 as a deliberately unified scene rather than a loose sequence of beats.

The decision explicitly flags that 'where poetry ends and prose resumes' is genuinely disputed and caps confidence at medium on that basis - and checking WEB's own paragraphing bears this out concretely rather than just abstractly: WEB actually breaks its paragraph between v.12 and v.13, separating the narrator's introduction-plus-quoted-imperative ('Sun, stand still on Gibeon...') from the continuation that reports the sun's compliance, cites the Book of Jashar, and supplies the theological gloss (vv.13-14, which WEB itself keeps together as one paragraph). I tested whether that means the decision should instead split v.12 from vv.13-14: the case against splitting is that v.13a (וַיִּדֹּם הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ, 'the sun stood still') is itself the direct grammatical fulfillment of the imperative just spoken - person shifts from second to third, but it is answering the very sentence v.12 quotes, the same command-fulfillment continuity that holds units together elsewhere in this campaign (8:18-19, 8:9). On balance the three verses cohere as one citation event (frame, quotation, fulfillment-with-source-note, and interpretive close), and WEB's break is best read as marking the seam between direct quotation and its narrated aftermath rather than a genuine scene division - which is precisely the ambiguity the decision already owns. primary_reviews.rationale: This is the decision that sets up the register/closure contrast the review brief asks me to adjudicate against ch.12, so I checked it against the full Hebrew text of both spans rather than the decision's own excerpts. It holds up: every one of the six city notices in 10:28-39 (Makkedah, Libnah, Lachish, Eglon, Hebron, Debir) carries individualized content beyond the proper name - day-counts that differ (Lachish 'on the second day,' Eglon 'that day'), an entirely extra episode at Lachish (Horam of Gezer's failed relief, with its own verb of arrival and its own defeat notice), a unique 'with all its cities' note at Hebron, and a shifting comparison target (Makkedah and Libnah both point back to Jericho, Eglon points to Lachish, Hebron to Eglon, and Debir closes with a double comparison to both Hebron and Libnah at once). That last detail - the comparison target drifting forward through the list rather than staying fixed on Jericho - is real and is itself evidence against reading these as a uniform template: a bare register would not bother varying its own cross-reference target. Makkedah's own comparative close (back to Jericho, not forward to Libnah) is exactly what the decision says and is the correct basis for treating v.28 as self-contained.

Makkedah does open the run differently: וְאֶת מַקֵּדָה֩ לָכַ֨ד יְהוֹשֻׁ֜עַ בַּיּ֣וֹם הַה֗וּא fronts the object before a bare qatal, against the march-formula that opens Libnah, Lachish and Eglon, and the same disjunctive shape reappears at 11:12's generalizing notice. Per-entry comparative closure is present here and absent from chapter 12, which is the discriminator that matters against the ch.12 analogy. One qualifier I would strike but do not challenge: the ALT says each entry names 'a different, migrating antecedent city,' and that fails at the first step - 10:28 and 10:30 both close by comparison with the king of Jericho. The discriminator does not depend on migration, only on each entry having a closure of its own, so the argument survives the deletion. Medium is right.

Makkedah's fronted-object-before-bare-qatal syntax (וְאֶת מַקֵּדָה֩ לָכַ֨ד יְהוֹשֻׁ֜עַ) is distinct from the motion-verb-plus-destination pattern used by the middle entries in this run, which I confirmed by checking Lachish (10:31, וַיַּעֲבֹר) and Hebron (10:36, וַיַּעַל) - both use a march verb rather than a fronted object. That makes Makkedah a deliberately marked opening beat for the southern campaign list, and closing it on its own comparative formula tying back to Jericho gives it a genuine discrete unit rather than an arbitrary first slice of a longer run.

Second, the rejected alternative's stated reason is false on the sequence: it calls 10:33 an interruption within the Lachish siege, but Lachish has already fallen in 10:32, captured בַּיּ֣וֹם הַשֵּׁנִ֔י and closed by its comparative formula, so 10:33 follows the capture rather than interrupting it. In fairness to the row, one consideration cuts the other way and I record it: Hebron at 10:37 also carries material after its comparative formula, so trailing content is not unprecedented. primary_reviews.rationale: This decision sits inside an unusually long unmarked stretch - checked the two-witness file and there is no pe or samekh anywhere between 12:8 and 13:14, and WEB does not break its paragraph at 13:7/8 either - so the discourse-mode shift (second-person imperative 'divide this land' giving way to third-person past-tense narration 'the Reubenites and Gadites received their inheritance') is genuinely the only signal available here, not one option among several external witnesses. That the rationale says so plainly ('no clear speech-closing formula appears') rather than overstating the evidence is itself a point in its favor. The shift from imperative to narrative is a real and recognized discourse-analysis boundary type, distinct from but structurally comparable to the speaker-change boundaries used throughout chs.7-9, and it is reasonable to rely on it here given the total absence of competing paragraph-level signals in this stretch.

The disclosure is the reason to support this row. 13:7 does end הַשְּׁבָטִ֑ים וַחֲצִ֖י הַשֵּׁ֥בֶט הַֽמְנַשֶּֽׁה and 13:8 does open on the bound עִמּ֗וֹ, so the unit's first word genuinely cannot be parsed without reaching back across the seam; the row states that, weighs it, and lowers the price for it rather than arguing it away. The discourse-mode shift from second-person imperative to third-person narration is a real counterweight. One caveat I note rather than file: 3:14 is offered as a precedent for a boundary without a formula, but 3:14 opens on the va-yehi-plus-infinitive device that M8-Josh-023 elsewhere calls a unit-opening construction, whereas 13:8 has no opener at all - so the parallel is weaker than the row implies. medium_low absorbs that.

This is an honestly unresolved seam and the row treats it that way rather than forcing a clean answer. The עִמּוֹ dependency is real - its antecedent genuinely sits at the end of v.7, so the unit's first word cannot be parsed in isolation - and rather than hide that, the row weighs it against the discourse-mode shift (second-person command to third-person narration) and explicitly lowers confidence to reflect the unresolved tension instead of resolving it by fiat. Declining to split v.7 mid-sentence to fix the dependency is also right, since that would fracture a single grammatical sentence for the sake of a tidier boundary. medium_low is the honest price for a seam this genuinely contested.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: No formal challenge; this row was already the more honestly hedged of the pair and the prose fix only tightens one comparison. Checked Josh.3.14 directly - it does open with its own vayehi-plus-infinitive-construct device (וַיְהִ֗י בִּנְסֹ֤עַ הָעָם֙), the same construction credited as unit-opening at M8-Josh-023 and matched independently at 1:1 and 4:1 - so treating 3:14 as a clean 'boundary without a formula' precedent for 13:8 was overstated. 13:8 itself has no such device, only the bound עִמּ֗וֹ reaching back to the antecedent at the end of 13:7 (וַחֲצִ֖י הַשֵּׁ֥בֶט הַֽמְנַשֶּֽׁה), confirmed. Removing the weaker precedent leaves the discourse-mode-shift argument to carry the seam alone, which is exactly what the row's own lowered medium_low price already reflects. No dispute.

peer_crosscheck_history.assessment: OL's challenge is grammatically sound and I would treat it as the most important unresolved point in this row. Josh.13.8 opens on עִמּוֹ, a bound preposition-plus-suffix whose antecedent, וַחֲצִי הַשֵּׁבֶט הַמְנַשֶּׁה, sits at the very end of 13:7 -- the preceding unit. This deserves an explicit accounting in the rationale, one way or the other, rather than silence.

primary_reviews.rationale: Two factual defects, both in the evidence rather than the span. The samekh cited as boundary evidence stands after Josh.13.32, but this unit runs Josh.13.32-Josh.13.33, so that marker falls between the unit's own two verses. It is an internal division in the Masoretic witness, not corroboration of an edge. Under the Prophets rule it cannot drive a split either way, so removing it costs nothing, but as filed it misstates where the witness sits. Separately, v.33 does not repeat v.14 verbatim. Collated: 13:14 reads רַ֚ק לְשֵׁ֣בֶט הַלֵּוִ֔י לֹ֥א נָתַ֖ן נַחֲלָ֑ה ... אִשֵּׁ֨י יְהוָ֜ה אֱלֹהֵ֤י יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ ה֣וּא נַחֲלָת֔וֹ, while 13:33 reads וּלְשֵׁ֨בֶט֙ הַלֵּוִ֔י לֹֽא נָתַ֥ן מֹשֶׁ֖ה נַחֲלָ֑ה ... יְהוָ֞ה אֱלֹהֵ֤י יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ ה֣וּא נַחֲלָתָ֔ם. Four differences - the restrictive particle against a conjunction, Moses supplied as explicit subject, the offerings-word dropped before the divine name, and the possessive suffix shifting from singular to plural. The inclusio reading survives all four; the word verbatim does not. Left edge (WEB paragraph at v.32, the summary opener) and the chapter-end right edge are otherwise sound, and medium is right.

primary_reviews.rationale: The inclusio reading of vv.32-33 bracketing the whole Transjordan section is sound and the samekh corroboration at 13:32 is correctly cited. But the specific factual claim that 'v.33 repeats the Levites'-no-inheritance formula verbatim from v.14' does not survive a character check. I pulled both verses from Josh_oshb.txt: 13:14 reads רַ֚ק לְשֵׁ֣בֶט הַלֵּוִ֔י לֹ֥א נָתַ֖ן נַחֲלָ֑ה אִשֵּׁ֨י יְהוָ֜ה אֱלֹהֵ֤י יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ ה֣וּא נַחֲלָת֔וֹ כַּאֲשֶׁ֖ר דִּבֶּר לֽוֹ, while 13:33 reads וּלְשֵׁ֨בֶט֙ הַלֵּוִ֔י לֹֽא נָתַ֥ן מֹשֶׁ֖ה נַחֲלָ֑ה יְהוָ֞ה אֱלֹהֵ֤י יִשְׂרָאֵל֙ ה֣וּא נַחֲלָתָ֔ם כַּאֲשֶׁ֖ר דִּבֶּ֥ר לָהֶֽם. Three real differences: (1) v.33 inserts מֹשֶׁה as an explicit subject where v.14 leaves the verb's subject implicit; (2) v.14 grounds the Levites' portion in אִשֵּׁי יְהוָה, 'the fire-offerings of Yahweh,' while v.33 drops אִשֵּׁי entirely and states directly that Yahweh himself is their inheritance, a theologically sharper formulation, not a copy; (3) the pronominal suffixes shift from singular (נַחֲלָתוֹ, לוֹ) to plural (נַחֲלָתָם, לָהֶם), tracking the shift from 'the tribe' as a collective singular subject to 'them' as the Levites collectively. This is a close formulaic echo, which is exactly the kind of resumptive repetition that legitimately brackets a section, but calling it verbatim overstates the case and could mislead a downstream reader checking Levitical-formula recurrence elsewhere in the book. The unit boundary itself (13:32-33 as the Transjordan section's shared close) is not in question; only the 'verbatim' characterization needs correcting to 'near-verbatim, with the offering-language dropped and the referents pluralized.'

primary_reviews.rationale: The conclusion may well be right; the argument for it is refuted by the text. The draft writes that v.21 immediately begins enumerating cities with no further introduction, so v.20 must belong with what it introduces. In fact v.21 opens with a full register heading: וַיִּֽהְי֣וּ הֶעָרִ֗ים מִקְצֵה֙ לְמַטֵּ֣ה בְנֵֽי יְהוּדָ֔ה אֶל גְּב֥וּל אֱד֖וֹם בַּנֶּ֑גְבָּה. That is the same construction the draft itself calls a fresh city-catalogue heading at M8-Josh-112, where 18:21 reads וְהָי֣וּ הֶֽעָרִ֗ים לְמַטֵּ֛ה בְּנֵ֥י בִנְיָמִ֖ן לְמִשְׁפְּחֽוֹתֵיהֶ֑ם - same verb root, same subject noun, same tribal prepositional phrase. v.21 therefore does not need v.20 to introduce it, and the stated ground collapses. What does support keeping v.20 with the register is evidence never cited here: the pe stands after Josh.15.19 rather than after 15.20, and WEB opens its paragraph at v.20 and runs straight into v.21, so both paragraphing witnesses put the seam at 19/20. Separately, calling this a uniform place-name catalogue understates it - v.25 carries the identification gloss חֶצְר֖וֹן הִ֥יא חָצֽוֹר and the closing numeral כָּל עָרִ֛ים עֶשְׂרִ֥ים וָתֵ֖שַׁע וְחַצְרֵיהֶֽן counts twenty-nine against roughly three dozen names actually enumerated in vv.21-32, a text-internal discrepancy of exactly the class the draft discloses for Hebron at M8-Josh-096 and leaves undisclosed here.

primary_reviews.rationale: The Wiederaufnahme heading at v.20 and the summarizing tally at v.32 both hold up against oshb. The Wiederaufnahme reading is the right call and is actually reinforced by comparing the two echoed phrases word for word: v.12 closes the border description with זֶה גְּבוּל בְּנֵי יְהוּדָה סָבִיב לְמִשְׁפְּחֹתָם while v.20 opens the resumed list with זֹאת נַחֲלַת מַטֵּה בְנֵי יְהוּדָה לְמִשְׁפְּחֹתָם - close enough in shape (same לְמִשְׁפְּחֹתָם tail, same near-demonstrative opener) to function as a recognizable echo-back after the Caleb-Achsah digression, but different enough in vocabulary (גְּבוּל/'border' vs נַחֲלַת/'inheritance', the added מַטֵּה, the dropped סָבִיב) that it reads as a genuine heading for what follows rather than a copy-paste duplicate of v.12. That distinction matters for the argument the decision makes (v.20 belongs with what it introduces, not what it echoes) and the near-but-not-identical wording is exactly what a Wiederaufnahme is supposed to look like. High confidence is earned three ways at once: the heading formula, the summarizing כָּל in the closing tally (כָּל עָרִים עֶשְׂרִים וָתֵשַׁע), and an independent samekh witness sitting at the exact close, v.15.32.

challenge_responses.response: Correct, and confirmed directly: Josh.15.21 reads וַיִּֽהְי֣וּ הֶעָרִ֗ים מִקְצֵה֙ לְמַטֵּ֣ה בְנֵֽי יְהוּדָ֔ה אֶל גְּב֥וּל אֱד֖וֹם בַּנֶּ֑גְבָּה, a full register-opening formula (verb הָיָה + הֶעָרִים + לְמַטֵּה + tribe name) - the same construction this draft calls a fresh city-catalogue heading at Josh.18.21 for M8-Josh-112. The premise that 'v.21 supplies no introduction of its own' is false on the draft's own terms. Replaced with the evidence that actually supports the placement: a pe is attested after Josh.15.19 (closing the preceding Achsah narrative) and WEB opens a paragraph at 15:20 that runs unbroken through v.21 rather than breaking between them. v.20's general resumption ('this is the inheritance of the tribe of the children of Judah') and v.21's specific city-list opening work together as a two-tier heading - a general Wiederaufnahme followed by the actual catalogue formula - rather than v.20 being read as the heading only because v.21 supposedly lacks one.

Confirmed: counting the named places in vv.21-32 (Kabzeel, Eder, Jagur ... through Hazor Hadattah, Kerioth Hezron/Hazor, Rimmon) yields roughly thirty-six names against the stated tally of twenty-nine at v.32, a real discrepancy plausibly tied to Hazor appearing both as a bare name (v.23) and inside a compound name (v.25). The rationale now discloses this openly, matching how the Hebron doubling is disclosed at M8-Josh-096, rather than passing over it silently.

Both verses carry a discrete per-entry closure formula: עָרִ֥ים שֵׁ֖שׁ וְחַצְרֵיהֶֽן and עָרִ֥ים שְׁתַּ֖יִם וְחַצְרֵיהֶֽן. The criterion says a discrete per-entry closure formula is decisive. primary_reviews.rationale: This is the writer-flagged decision and it deserves the scrutiny it asks for. The Hebrew is accurate (v.58, v.59, v.60 all check against oshb), and the WEB-paragraphing claim is also accurate as description: I traced every ¶(m) marker across the whole chapter and confirmed resets at vv.33, 37, 42, 45, 48, 52, 55, 58, and 61 (Josh_web_clean.txt lines 548-585) - nine breaks, one at the start of every terrain- or tally-cluster from v.33 through v.61, with v.58 getting its own ¶(m) and v.60 genuinely not getting one, exactly as the decision states. The problem is what that fact is being asked to do. Every other multi-tally stretch in this chapter is split by the numeral alone, with the terrain heading or WEB's paragraphing treated as irrelevant to the split: M8-Josh-091/092/093 explicitly split three lowland clusters that all share one unstated שְׁפֵלָה heading and get separate WEB ¶(m) marks anyway, and M8-Josh-095/096/097 do the same for hill country. Verses 58-59 close with עָרִים שֵׁשׁ וְחַצְרֵיהֶן ('six cities') and v.60 closes with עָרִים שְׁתַּיִם וְחַצְרֵיהֶן ('two cities') - two discrete per-entry closure formulas, structurally identical in kind to the ones that drove every prior split in this chapter. Under the register-closure criterion as stated ('discrete per-entry closure formula decisive'), that should be decisive here too. Instead the rationale's stated reason for not splitting is that 'WEB's own paragraphing keeps them together' - which inverts the rule's own hierarchy: WEB paragraphing is listed alongside marker-only evidence as insufficient to drive a decision, while a discrete closure formula is supposed to be decisive. There is also an available and uncited two-witness samekh mark at exactly 15:60 (confirmed in the parashah_two_witness.json samekh site list), which if anything corroborates the split the rule's own criterion calls for, not the merge that was adopted. I don't think the honesty of the hedge ('a judgment call, not a confident boundary') resolves this, because the inconsistency is with the chapter's own established practice, not just with an abstract standard - the same drafter treated formally identical situations differently five times over (091-093, 095-097 split; 098 merges) without a text-internal reason for the exception.

primary_reviews.rationale: Two problems, one of them the parallel the brief singles out. The draft asserts that this notice is matched at 16:10 and 17:12-13 and treats all three as one literary type. In Hebrew they are not one construction. 15:63 reads לֹֽא יוכלו יָכְל֥וּ בְנֵֽי יְהוּדָ֖ה לְהֽוֹרִישָׁ֑ם and 17:12 reads וְלֹ֤א יָכְלוּ֙ בְּנֵ֣י מְנַשֶּׁ֔ה לְהוֹרִ֖ישׁ - both are the verb of ability plus an infinitive of dispossession, statements of incapacity with an explicit tribal subject. 16:10 reads וְלֹ֣א הוֹרִ֔ישׁוּ אֶת הַֽכְּנַעֲנִ֖י הַיּוֹשֵׁ֣ב בְּגָ֑זֶר: no verb of ability at all, no explicit subject, a plain negated hiphil reporting non-performance rather than inability. The closing clauses group differently again. 16:10 ends וַיְהִ֖י לְמַס עֹבֵֽד and 17:13 ends וַיִּתְּנ֥וּ אֶת הַֽכְּנַעֲנִ֖י לָמַ֑ס וְהוֹרֵ֖שׁ לֹ֥א הוֹרִישֽׁוֹ, both forced-labour outcomes, while 15:63 alone closes on coexistence, וַיֵּ֨שֶׁב הַיְבוּסִ֜י אֶת בְּנֵ֤י יְהוּדָה֙ בִּיר֣וּשָׁלִַ֔ם עַ֖ד הַיּ֥וֹם הַזֶּֽה. So the real pairing runs 15:63 with 17:12 on the verb and 16:10 with 17:13 on the outcome, and 17:12-13 contains both constructions at once. Second defect: the ketiv/qere is printed but not annotated, the ref carrying the unpointed and pointed forms as an undifferentiated string. The boundary itself is fine - pe after Josh.15.63, WEB paragraph at 62/63, wayyiqtol prose against a numeral-closed catalogue - and medium is the right price.

primary_reviews.rationale: The merge is asserted on a referent that does not hold. The stated reason is that v.9's enclave cities are themselves the subject whose Canaanite inhabitants v.10 says could not be driven out. v.9's cities are וְהֶעָרִ֗ים הַמִּבְדָּלוֹת֙ לִבְנֵ֣י אֶפְרַ֔יִם בְּת֖וֹךְ נַחֲלַ֣ת בְּנֵֽי מְנַשֶּׁ֑ה - set apart inside Manasseh's inheritance. v.10's object is the Canaanite dwelling in Gezer, and Gezer is not among them: it appears at 16:3 as a terminus on the Joseph tribes' own southern line, וְעַד גָּ֑זֶר. The two verses concern different places. Compounding this, v.9 closes with a register tag of its own, כָּֽל הֶעָרִ֖ים וְחַצְרֵיהֶֽן - the uncounted variant of the closure formula this draft treats as decisive throughout ch.15 - which the decision neither quotes nor weighs, and which is precisely the independent right edge a standalone v.9 would require. The outer edges of the span are fine, with the Ephraim colophon behind and the pe after Josh.16.10 ahead, so this challenges the internal merge and its stated ground, not where the unit begins and ends.

primary_reviews.rationale: The enclave-cities notice at v.9 and the Gezer failure-notice at v.10 square with oshb line for line. This decision's subject-continuity argument (the enclave cities of v.9 are the very cities whose Canaanite residents v.10 says could not be dispossessed) is textually sound and is a better basis for merging list-material with narrative than mere adjacency would be. It is also the one failure-notice decision that already partially self-corrects the type-family overclaim challenged at M8-Josh-107: it explicitly notes the forced-labor clause (וַיְהִי לְמַס עֹבֵד) as new content 15:63 lacked, rather than asserting flat identity. primary_reviews.rationale: The new singleton is well made. Its construction really is distinct from its two family members - וְלֹ֣א הוֹרִ֔ישׁוּ is an unmodalized negated Hiphil with no ability verb - and its coda pairs a 'to this day' clause with a corvee outcome that 15:63 does not have. The row is candid that its existence is what makes M8-Josh-107's family claim true rather than merely asserted, which is the sort of cross-row bookkeeping that should be visible. Pe after 16:10 is tagged as weak. Medium is consistent with the other two members of the family.

As the companion correction to 103, this row is right for the same reason in reverse: v.10's plain unmodalized וְלֹא הוֹרִישׁוּ, its 'to this day' notice, and its forced-labor outcome (וַיְהִ֖י לְמַס עֹבֵֽד) are a self-contained failure-notice with no dependence on v.9's enclave-cities material. I confirmed the pe after 16:10 is genuinely present. Once the false referent-based merge is corrected, this notice functions exactly like 15:63 and 17:12-13 - a discrete beat within the recurring failure-to-dispossess family - and treating it that way makes the family principle actually consistent across all three instances rather than true in name only.

peer_crosscheck.assessment: The construction-class distinction this row rests on is real. Josh.16.10 opens with a plain negated Hiphil perfect, וְלֹ֣א הוֹרִ֔ישׁוּ, no modal auxiliary; checked both comparison verses directly and 15:63 reads לֹֽא יָכְל֥וּ בְנֵֽי יְהוּדָ֖ה לְהֽוֹרִישָׁ֑ם while 17:12 reads וְלֹ֤א יָכְלוּ֙ בְּנֵ֣י מְנַשֶּׁ֔ה לְהוֹרִ֖ישׁ - both genuinely built on the modal יָכְלוּ ('were able') plus an infinitive, a different construction from 16:10's own. The forced-labor coda, וַיְהִ֖י לְמַ֥ס עֹבֵֽד, and the 'to this day' notice are both confirmed present and absent from 15:63's parallel notice. The claim that Gezer is not one of v.9's named enclave cities also holds: 16:9 (M8-Josh-103) names no cities at all, only an uncounted, unenumerated 'cities and their villages' tag, so Gezer's only prior explicit mention is indeed 16:3's border reference. The bookkeeping claim about M8-Josh-107 checks out too - that row's own text names 16:10 as 'now its own decision, M8-Josh-164,' confirming the family-of-three principle is actually realized rather than asserted. Pe after 16:10 confirmed present. No dispute; medium matches its two family members.

Unlike 089, this insert is not corroborated by an external witness site, but it has its own internal legal-precedent cross-reference the drafter could have cited and didn't: the request 'Yahweh commanded Moses to give us an inheritance' (v.4) explicitly invokes the Numbers 27/36 precedent by name of act rather than narrating it fresh, meaning this passage functions as a citation of prior law applied to a new administrative moment, not a standalone story - a slightly different insert-type than Caleb's autobiographical petition, worth distinguishing for the document-poetics record even though it doesn't change the boundary call. primary_reviews.rationale: The span itself (17:12-13 as one unit, separate from the border description before it and Joseph's complaint after it) is well supported and I would keep it - in fact it is better supported by content than by WEB's own paragraphing, which actually breaks between v.12 and v.13 while grouping v.13 with v.14 (¶ at Josh_web_clean.txt line 618, none between 619 and 620), the opposite seam from the one the decision draws. The decision is right to override that grouping: v.14 opens with וַֽיְדַבְּרוּ֙ בְּנֵ֣י יוֹסֵ֔ף...לֵאמֹ֑ר, the same direct-speech-introduction formula the sibling decision at 108 correctly identifies as its own opening marker, so v.13's material belongs with the failure-and-forced-labor report at v.12, not with the complaint at v.14, regardless of what WEB's paragraph break suggests. What I am challenging is a specific factual claim, not the span: the rejected-alternative section states that the three failure-to-dispossess notices (15:63, 16:10, 17:12-13) show 'nothing in the text itself differentiates their closural force from one occurrence to the next.' That is not accurate. I compared all three constructions directly. 15:63 and 17:12 share the modal construction לֹא + יָכְלוּ (perfect) + subject + לְהוֹרִישׁ(ם) (infinitive) - 'were not able to dispossess.' 16:10 instead uses a direct, unmodalized Hiphil, וְלֹא הוֹרִישׁוּ - 'they did not dispossess' - a formally different construction, not a stylistic variant of the same one. The codas differ further: 15:63 closes with a bare 'to this day' dwelling notice; 16:10 adds a forced-labor tag (וַיְהִי לְמַס עֹבֵד) that 15:63 lacks; and 17:12-13 alone closes with a distinct 'the Canaanite was resolved to dwell in this land' clause (וַיּוֹאֶל הַכְּנַעֲנִי לָשֶׁבֶת בָּאָרֶץ הַזֹּאת, found nowhere else) followed by an entirely separate v.13 clause introduced by its own temporal formula וַיְהִי כִּי חָזְקוּ ('and it happened, when Israel grew strong') and closing on an emphatic infinitive-absolute construction, וְהוֹרֵשׁ לֹא הוֹרִישׁוֹ ('but they did not utterly dispossess it'), which has no counterpart at all in the other two notices. That is three distinguishable closural shapes, not one undifferentiated type, and 17:12-13's two-stage structure (immediate failure, then a later, separately-dated subjugation) is the most elaborate of the three. None of this unseats the span or the decision to keep the three notices as separate units rather than absorbing them into their surrounding border/list material - it only unseats the specific claim that their closural force is textually indistinguishable, which matters because that claim is being used as the stated warrant for treating the type consistently rather than case-by-case.

primary_reviews.rationale: The outer edges are impeccable - lot formula at וַיַּ֗עַל גּוֹרַ֛ל מַטֵּ֥ה בְנֵֽי בִנְיָמִ֖ן לְמִשְׁפְּחֹתָ֑ם, inheritance colophon at זֹ֡את נַחֲלַת֩ בְּנֵ֨י בִנְיָמִ֧ן לִגְבֽוּלֹתֶ֛יהָ סָבִ֖יב לְמִשְׁפְּחֹתָֽם, pe after Josh.18.10 immediately behind. The rejected alternative rests on a statement the text refutes: that none of Benjamin's internal directional headings supplies its own sub-colophon. Two of them do. The west section ends זֹ֖את פְּאַת יָֽם at v.14 and the south section ends זֶ֖ה גְּב֥וּל נֶֽגֶב at v.19, and v.15 reopens with the fresh cardinal heading וּפְאַת נֶ֕גְבָּה. The v.19 tag is materially the clause on which M8-Josh-087 splits Judah's border at 15:4. The two decisions therefore take opposite readings of one signal type and both are priced high. Whichever way the campaign resolves it - sub-colophons cut, and Benjamin divides; or they do not, and Judah's 15:1-12 recombines - one of these two high prices has to move. This is the single most consequential inconsistency I found across clusters 11-15.

primary_reviews.rationale: High is earned here, and I checked both edges separately. Near edge: 18:11 opens the tribal lot formula, וַיַּ֗עַל גּוֹרַ֛ל מַטֵּ֥ה בְנֵֽי בִנְיָמִ֖ן, which is the opener class used for every allotment in this section. Far edge: 18:14 ends זֹ֖את פְּאַת יָֽם, a deictic-plus-border-noun tag of exactly the shape credited high at Judah's 15:4 (יָ֑מָּה זֶה יִהְיֶ֥ה לָכֶ֖ם גְּב֥וּל נֶֽגֶב). Those are independent of one another, so the both-edges bar is met on text signals alone with no marker in sight. The claim that the old span rested on a falsehood is also true - 18:14 and 18:19 both carry closing tags, so 'no internal directional heading supplies its own closing tag' could not stand.

This is a well-earned high-confidence call: I checked 18:14's closing tag against Judah's 15:4 directly and the deictic-plus-border-noun construction (זֹאת/זֶה + פְּאַת/גְּבוּל) genuinely matches, giving this west-quarter sub-unit both a strong opening lot-formula and a cross-tribally corroborated closing tag. The correction to the prior 'no internal directional heading carries its own closing tag' claim is factually necessary - I checked and 18:14 and 18:19 plainly do each close on independent deictic tags - so splitting Benjamin's border description into three sub-units (west, south, east-plus-colophon) rather than one undivided span is the more accurate mapping of the text's own three-part structure, not an arbitrary subdivision for its own sake.

This single verse completing Benjamin's border with the Jordan as the east quarter, then sealing the whole tribal unit on the standard נַחֲלַת-colophon, is a complete literary beat even though it is brief - I checked the closing formula against the pattern used to close every other tribal unit in this section and it matches exactly. A colophon-plus-final-geographic-notice compressed into one verse is a recognized convention in this material, not an awkward truncation, so treating it as its own decision rather than folding it into 160's south-quarter unit correctly separates the tribe's final seal from the preceding directional description. medium appropriately reflects a brief opening notice paired with the strongest closing signal available anywhere in this campaign.

No dispute; medium is right for a brief opening notice paired with the strongest colophon type in the section.

primary_reviews.rationale: The city-catalogue heading at v.21 and the twelve-city tally at v.24 hold up against oshb, and the genre transition (border-perambulation genre to place-name-list genre) is correctly identified. But I don't think the high confidence rating is earned on the closing edge, and it is worth flagging precisely because the instructions ask for scrutiny of unearned highs. This unit's closure is a bare numeral, עָרִים שְׁתֵּים עֶשְׂרֵה וְחַצְרֵיהֶן ('twelve cities'), with no נַחֲלַת-colophon of its own - it shares its heading (v.21's וְהָיוּ הֶעָרִים...) with the second Benjamin city cluster at M8-Josh-113 (18:25-28) exactly the way the three lowland clusters at M8-Josh-091/092/093 share their unstated שְׁפֵלָה heading, and exactly the way the three hill-country clusters at M8-Josh-095/096/097 share theirs. Every one of those five structurally identical cases (a shared or absent heading plus a bare tally-only closure) was rated medium. This decision, with the same structural profile on its closing edge, is rated high. The opening edge here is admittedly stronger than 091's bare 'in the lowland' tag - v.21 restates the tribe's full name - but the rule requires both edges independently evidenced for a high rating, and the closing edge is exactly as thin as the ones that kept five comparable decisions at medium. primary_reviews.rationale: The seventh-lot opener at v.40, the Leshem notice at v.47, and the colophon at v.48 all square with oshb, and the pe witness at 19:48 is confirmed. This decision is worth stress-testing directly against the Caleb-Achsah insert at M8-Josh-089, since both involve a narrative episode embedded in list material, and they are handled differently - correctly so, on inspection. The Caleb insert opens with a topic-fronted, named-individual construction (וּלְכָלֵב בֶּן יְפֻנֶּה נָתַן חֵלֶק) introducing a new personal subject distinct from the list's collective voice, which is why it earns its own decision. The Leshem episode at 19:47 introduces no new subject at all - בְּנֵי דָן is the same collective tribal subject that has governed the whole unit since v.40, and the verse simply continues the ordinary wayyiqtol narrative chain (וַיַּעֲלוּ...וַיִּלָּחֲמוּ...וַיִּלְכְּדוּ) with no topic-fronting or reintroduction formula. That is a real, checkable difference in kind, not just in length, and it is why folding the Leshem material into Dan's unit while carving Caleb's material out as its own unit is methodologically consistent rather than arbitrary. WEB agrees, marking no internal break across vv.40-48 (no ¶ between Josh_web_clean.txt lines 708 and 718).

primary_reviews.rationale: Joshua's own-inheritance notice at v.50 and the grand colophon at v.51 hold up against oshb, and the pe witness at 19:51 is confirmed. This is the strongest colophon-architecture finding in the whole cluster set: I compared the officiating body named at 19:51 against the one named at 14:1, and they match closely enough to function as a deliberate ring - אֶלְעָזָר הַכֹּהֵן וִיהוֹשֻׁעַ בִּן נוּן וְרָאשֵׁי אֲבוֹת הַמַּטּוֹת לִבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל at 14:1 versus אֶלְעָזָר הַכֹּהֵן וִיהוֹשֻׁעַ בִּן נוּן וְרָאשֵׁי הָאָבוֹת לְמַטּוֹת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל at 19:51, the same three-party body (priest, commander, tribal heads) named in the same order at both the opening superscription of the whole Cisjordan allotment and its closing colophon. primary_reviews.rationale: The execution notice is soundly bounded. וַיַּקְדִּ֜שׁוּ opens with a wayyiqtol that switches the text from prescription to performance, and the closing formula אֵ֣לֶּה הָיוּ֩ עָרֵ֨י הַמּֽוּעָדָ֜ה verifies exactly, including the extension of asylum to the resident alien that the draft highlights. The far edge carries no marker, which under the Prophets rule counts for nothing either way, and it needs none: v.32 opens with a return journey and a change of place, independent evidence of the seam. primary_reviews.rationale: The closing unit of the altar dispute is soundly bounded and the high band is warranted. The return journey relocates the scene, and the narrative ends on the naming etiology, כִּ֣י עֵ֥ד הוּא֙ בֵּֽינֹתֵ֔ינוּ כִּ֥י יְהוָ֖ה הָאֱלֹהִֽים, quoted exactly. Each edge is independently supported - a movement of participants and place at one end, a naming formula plus the close of the chapter at the other - and the two-witness file records a pe after 22:34 which the draft could have cited and did not. Worth entering for consistency with this cluster's own practice at 21:36-37: the Masoretic text as printed supplies no actual name for the altar in v.34, the clause running straight from the verb of naming to the causal 'for it is a witness'. primary_reviews.rationale: The Joseph notice stands on its own and the reasoning is sound. It opens with וְאֶת עַצְמ֣וֹת י֠וֹסֵף, a fronted accusative that suspends the expected verb order and signals a new subject rather than a continuation, and it closes with וַיִּֽהְי֥וּ לִבְנֵֽי יוֹסֵ֖ף לְנַחֲלָֽה, a clause resolving the notice grammatically instead of trailing into what follows. The change of burial place and of legal basis - a purchase from Hamor's sons rather than an allotted city - is real and is used correctly. The following verse opens with the same fronted construction, so the far edge is marked by the device that marks the near edge, unusually tidy for a one-verse unit. The middle band is right; a singleton whose edges are both syntactic rather than formulaic should not be priced at the top.

וְאֶת עַצְמ֣וֹת י֠וֹסֵף...קָבְר֣וּ בִשְׁכֶם֒ verified verbatim. This is the cleanest test in the cluster of the rule that marker absence must not count as counter-evidence: WEB places no paragraph break at all between v.31 and v.32, yet the content-based case for splitting is strong on its own terms — new named subject (Joseph rather than Joshua), a different burial location tied to a different legal event (Jacob's purchase, not Timnath-serah), and its own independent closing clause וַיִּֽהְי֥וּ לִבְנֵֽי יוֹסֵ֖ף לְנַחֲלָֽה.
